ruleIntents.intent: Checks the existence and non-emptiness of an HTML page's <title>, NOT its descriptiveness. Concretely it verifies two things: (a) the root html element of a non-embedded page has at least one descendant <title> element anywhere in the document tree, and (b) the FIRST such <title> in document order contains text-node children that are not whitespace-only. A page with no <title>, an empty <title></title>, or a <title> containing only whitespace/separator characters fails. It is a pure DOM-tree structural/text-presence check (Input Aspect: DOM Tree only); no rendering, no semantics, no comparison against page content.
ruleIntents.scLimb: 2.4.2 Page Titled has effectively two limbs: (1) a title EXISTS, and (2) the title DESCRIBES the page topic/purpose. This rule exercises ONLY limb (1) — that a title is present and non-empty. It deliberately does NOT test the descriptiveness/topic-or-purpose limb (the rule's own Related Rules and Other Resources defer that to the separate "HTML page title is descriptive" rule and to G88). So a page can pass 2779a5 yet still fail SC 2.4.2 if the title is non-empty but uninformative.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to the ROOT element of the web page only if that root element is an html element (i.e., a non-embedded, top-level HTML document). It is therefore inapplicable when the root is not html (e.g., a standalone SVG document, as in the inapplicable test case), and inapplicable to HTML embedded via iframe/object since those are not "web pages" per WCAG. Title elements inside embedded content, inside SVG, or inside a shadow root (not a descendant of the document element) do not count toward the applicable html root.
ruleIntents.expectation: Two cumulative expectations on each target html root: Expectation 1 — it has at least one descendant <title> element. Expectation 2 — the first <title> that is a descendant of the document element has children that are text nodes which are not only whitespace. Both must hold to pass. Outcome mapping: any failure => SC 2.4.2 not satisfied; all-passed => SC needs further testing (descriptiveness still unverified); inapplicable => needs further testing.
scenarioTypesPresent: Pass: html root with a non-empty <title> (title placed directly under <html>, no <head>, single text node)
Fail: html root with NO <title> element at all (only an <h1>)
Inapplicable: root element is not <html> (standalone SVG document whose only <title> belongs to the svg, not an html page)
syntheticNarrowness: Each fixture is a 3-4 line skeleton: a bare <html> with no <head>, no <body> in the pass/fail cases, no DOCTYPE-meaningful content, no real page body, no CSS, no scripts, no charset/lang/meta — nothing resembling a production document where the <title> lives in <head> alongside meta tags and where surrounding markup could confuse a detector

The pass case uses a trivially literal title 'This page has a title' — it never tests the gap between this rule (presence) and the actual SC (descriptiveness): no fixture has a present-but-useless title like 'Untitled', 'Document', 'index', 'Home', a bare brand name, or boilerplate identical across pages, all of which pass this rule yet violate real SC 2.4.2

The empty/whitespace failure modes that the rule text explicitly enumerates (empty <title></title>, whitespace-only, single separator character like '-' or '|') are NOT represented in this subset — only the most blunt no-title-element-at-all failure is sampled, so the 'first title is whitespace-only' branch of Expectation 2 is untested by these cases

The interesting placement/ordering edge cases from the rule's own examples are absent: title in <body> instead of <head>, multiple <title> elements where only the first matters, two titles where the first is empty and the second has content (a fail), and the shadow-DOM template case where the title is not a descendant of the document element

The iframe/object distinction central to applicability is not exercised: no fixture has a parent page whose title titles an embedded child, nor an embedded child whose title must be ignored — the applicability boundary is only probed via the SVG-root case, missing the embedded-HTML dimension entirely

Real-world title variety is unsampled: dynamically/JS-injected titles, titles set via frameworks/SPA routing after load, titles containing only entities or emoji, very long titles, duplicate titles across a site, titles localized per lang, and server-rendered <head> with conditional templating — the static 3-line DOM gives no signal about any runtime or content-quality dimension

The inapplicable case conflates two reasons (non-html root AND title-belongs-to-svg) into one fixture; there is no clean isolation of 'applicable html root that merely also contains an svg <title>' versus 'truly inapplicable non-html root', so a detector could pass the subset by keying on the literal <svg root tag rather than the general not-an-html-root rule

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that the FIRST <title> element of an HTML document is semantically descriptive of the topic/purpose of the page's overall content — i.e. it is a content-relevance judgment on the title text, not a presence/non-emptiness check. The page body asserts a known topic ("Clementines will be ready to harvest..."), and the rule's verdict turns on whether the title's words match that topic. Passing requires the title to actually name the subject (e.g. "Clementine harvesting season"); failing means the title is present and non-empty but topically wrong or merely generic (a sibling fruit "Apple harvesting season", or a bare site name "University of Arkham" for a search-results page). This requires natural-language semantic comparison of title-vs-content, which is why the rule is implementable manual/semi-auto, not purely auto.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 2.4.2 Page Titled has effectively two conjoined obligations: (a) the page HAS a title, and (b) the title DESCRIBES topic or purpose. This rule exercises ONLY limb (b) — the descriptiveness/relevance limb. The presence/non-empty limb (a) is explicitly carved out: pages with no title or whitespace-only titles are INAPPLICABLE here and are delegated to the sibling rule "HTML page has non-empty title". So this rule presupposes a non-empty title exists and judges solely whether its content is meaningful and on-topic.
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to the document title of each HTML web page — operationally, the FIRST <title> element of the top-level document. Excluded (inapplicable) when: the page has no document title; the title contains only whitespace text nodes; or the title belongs to an embedded/non-web-page document context (title inside svg, iframe, or object), since those are not "web pages" per WCAG. Accessibility-support note: only the first <title> is considered (browsers honor the first), so second-and-later title elements are ignored regardless of placement. Notably a <title> placed in <body> instead of <head> IS still applicable, because the browser repairs it.
ruleIntents.expectation: The target element (first document title) describes the topic or purpose of the overall content of the document. Pass = title text is topically relevant to the page content; Fail = title is present and non-empty but does not describe the content (wrong subject, or generic/site-name-only). Outcome mapping: any fail => SC not satisfied; all pass => SC satisfied; inapplicable => SC needs further testing.
scenarioTypesPresent: Pass: single title whose words directly name the page topic (title matches body subject)
Pass: multiple titles where the FIRST is correct and the descriptiveness of the second is irrelevant (first-title-only rule)
Pass: title element misplaced in <body> rather than <head>, still descriptive (DOM-repair tolerance)
Fail: present non-empty title naming a closely-related-but-wrong subject (Apple vs Clementine — semantic near-miss, not gibberish)
Fail: multiple titles where the FIRST is wrong even though a later title is correct (first-title-only enforcement)
Fail: generic/uninformative title that is real but non-descriptive (bare website/organization name on a search-results page)
Inapplicable: <title> nested in an svg (embedded non-web-page document)
syntheticNarrowness: All pages are trivially short single-paragraph fixtures with one obvious topic word; real pages have long, multi-section, mixed-topic content where 'describes the topic/purpose of the OVERALL content' is genuinely ambiguous — none of that judgment difficulty is exercised here.

The fail cases are caricatured: an exact wrong sibling fruit ('Apple' vs 'Clementine') and a bare org name. Real-world borderline failures (titles that are partially relevant, overly long keyword-stuffed SEO titles, truncated titles, titles describing only part of the page) are absent.

Every page is English-only with lang='en'; the rule declares Language as a required input aspect, yet no non-English or wrong-lang title case tests whether descriptiveness is judged in the document's language.

Title content is always a clean human-readable phrase; common real patterns are missing — empty-ish placeholders ('Untitled Document', 'Document', 'Home', 'index'), template leftovers ('%PAGE_TITLE%', 'React App'), or site-name-prefix patterns ('Acme | Login') where the descriptive part is buried.

Inapplicability is shown via exactly ONE embedded-context variant (svg title). The other named exclusions — title inside iframe or object, no-title-at-all, and whitespace-only title — have no fixture in this corpus, so the boundary with the sibling 'non-empty title' rule is untested.

The multi-title scenarios are clean two-title pairs in <head>; they don't test the interaction of misplaced + duplicated titles, or whitespace-only first title followed by a real second title (which would flip applicability).

There is no dynamic/SPA scenario: real titles are frequently set or mutated by JavaScript after load (document.title updates on route change). All fixtures are static server-rendered HTML, so client-side title generation — a major real-world source of 2.4.2 failures — is entirely uncovered.

The 'purpose' half of 'topic OR purpose' is never isolated: every pass hinges on topical word-overlap. A page whose title describes its functional purpose (e.g. a checkout form, a contact page) rather than a subject noun is not represented.

scLimbsCoveredByACT: Existence / non-empty title (TT 12.A 'A element is defined'): covered by rule 2779a5. Passed cases give a title element with content (7f9f315b 'This page has a title'; efa1e0 / 6b3d2e2 title in body; 64771c title on iframe-parent). Failed cases cover the explicit absence/empty enumerations: no title element at all (820fb18 <h1>this page has no title</h1>), empty <title> (314d991), whitespace-only (4eeff9 — maps to F25 'Empty text'), first-of-two title empty (a149686), iframe title not counting for host page (5fd6fda).

Title describes topic or purpose (TT 12.B / F25 'title does not identify the contents'): covered by rule c4a8a4. Pass = title matches body content ('Clementine harvesting season' over clementine-harvest paragraph: c19c231, 2f970957). Fail = title names the wrong subject ('Apple harvesting season' over clementine content: 2c139703) — a direct F25 'does not identify the contents' instance.

Browser/algorithm title resolution = which title element counts (Understanding implies a single page title; c4a8a4 'browsers only recognize the first title element'): covered. First-of-two-titles is the one judged for both existence (2779a5 a149686, 0ad882d) and descriptiveness (c4a8a4 107a5e 'Second title is ignored' passes, 1844d7b 'First title is incorrect' fails).

Applicability boundary: title belongs to a web page, not an embedded/non-page document (Understanding ties the SC to a 'web page'; 2779a5/c4a8a4 background excludes iframe/object/svg). Covered by both inapplicable cases (ecc29b73 / 85469fd: <title> inside a standalone <svg>) and the iframe failures (5fd6fda host has no own title; 9c5eeb shadow-root title not a descendant of the document element).

Generic / non-distinguishing title as a descriptiveness failure (F25 'title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages' / 'authoring default titles'): partially covered by c4a8a4 4c72b3b — title 'University of Arkham' is a generic site name that does not describe the actual page ('Search results for accessibility').
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: The 'set of web pages' / uniqueness limb is NOT exercised as a multi-page check. The Understanding's central example (the entire APG title hierarchy: 'Patterns | APG | WAI | W3C' etc.), TT 12.B step 2 ('part of a set of web pages, determine whether the Page Title is sufficient to distinguish the web page from other pages') and the F25 'templated identical title across pages' example require comparing >1 page. Every ACT case is a single standalone page, so cross-page distinctiveness is structurally untestable in this corpus. (4c72b3b touches non-descriptiveness but is judged intra-page, not against siblings.)

Single Page Application (SPA) dynamic title change — Understanding para 3 ('various distinct pages/views all nominally served from the same URI ... the title of the page should also be changed dynamically to reflect the content or topic of the current view'). No case has JS that mutates document.title on view change; the one script case (9c5eeb) only attaches a shadow root and is about title-element scoping, not dynamic retitling.

Title supplied by a higher-level protocol / non-HTML technology — 2779a5 assumption ('the title of the page is not provided by a higher-level protocol ... subject field of an email ... rule will fail while SC 2.4.2 may still be satisfied'), plus F25/G88 'All technologies' and EN C.9.2.4.2 'is, or includes, a web page'. No PDF, no email-HTML, no SVG-as-standalone-document-with-title, no protocol-provided title case exists; SVG only appears as an inapplicable non-page.

'Document or web application name is sufficient' limb — Understanding para 2 and TT 12.B.b ('For documents or web applications, the name of the document or web application would be sufficient'). No case presents a document-name or application-name title (e.g. 'Bank XYZ, accounts for Alex Smith' from the Understanding's banking example). Descriptiveness is only ever tested against article body prose.

G88's qualitative sub-limbs: 'Make sense when read out of context (screen reader / site map / search-results list)' and 'Be short'. No case probes an over-long title, a title that is content-correct but meaningless out of context, or a title-vs-link-text continuity check (Understanding's 2.4.4/2.4.9 cross-reference). Descriptiveness is binary subject-match only.

G127 advisory limb — identifying the page's relationship to a larger collection, whether via the title's site/sub-site/chapter naming OR via rel/link metadata. No case includes collection-relationship metadata or a multi-part collection title, so the advisory technique is wholly unrepresented.

F25 'placeholder / authoring-default title' as an explicit descriptiveness failure ('Untitled Document', 'New Page 1', 'Enter the title of your HTML document here', non-descriptive filenames like report.html). These are listed verbatim in F25 but no ACT case uses such a placeholder/default string — the descriptiveness failures use a plausibly-real but wrong-subject title instead.
contentDomainsPresent: Bare/structural HTML skeletons (the dominant 'domain' — most 2779a5 cases are just <html><title>...</title></html> with no body content)
Short informational article / prose snippet (horticulture: 'Clementine/Apple harvesting season' paragraph) — the only real body content, used for all descriptiveness cases
Search-results page (single c4a8a4 case 4c72b3b: 'Search results for accessibility at the University of Arkham', body says 'None')
Embedded-document patterns: iframe with src to a sub-asset page (5fd6fda, 64771c, 94ff40)
Inline SVG graphic with a <title> (ecc29b, 85469fd) — used as the inapplicable boundary, not as page content
Shadow DOM / template + script (9c5eeb) — DOM-scoping edge case, not a content domain
varietyGaps: No multi-page / site-set scenario at all — the single biggest gap. The SC's headline distinguish-within-a-set limb and the F25 templated-identical-title failure cannot be represented by 20 isolated single-page fixtures.
No dynamic / scripted title behaviour reflecting the SC's SPA clause — no document.title mutation on route/view change; titles are 100% static markup.
No non-HTML / higher-level-protocol title sources (PDF document, HTML email subject, standalone SVG document title) despite F25/G88 stating 'All technologies' and the 2779a5 protocol assumption.

Descriptiveness is tested with a single, very narrow rubric: wrong-subject title over a one-paragraph horticulture article. No length/verbosity failures, no out-of-context-meaningless titles, no authoring-default placeholders ('Untitled Document', 'New Page 1'), no document/web-application-name-as-title acceptance case, no title-vs-link-text continuity.

Extremely thin content/UI variety: no forms, tables, navigation, media, multi-section pages, or any realistic application UI. Almost every fixture is an artificial markup stub authored to probe the title-resolution algorithm (which-title-element-counts, head vs body, first-of-two, iframe/svg/shadow boundaries) rather than realistic pages a real audit would see.
G127's metadata route (rel/link element, collection-position metadata) and any collection-relationship title is entirely unrepresented.

Language/i18n variety is absent: every descriptive case is English ('lang=en'); no non-Latin script, RTL, or mismatched-lang title to test that descriptiveness judgement (which depends on the 'Language' input aspect c4a8a4 declares) generalizes.

aspects.title: Non-empty but meaningless title: authoring-tool default, filename, or filler text
aspects.description: The page has fully developed, specific content (an article, product page, form), but the <title> is an IDE/CMS leftover or filler: 'Untitled Document', 'No Title', 'New Page 1', 'Enter the title of your HTML document here', a non-descriptive filename like 'spk12.html' or 'recipe-final-v2.html', or generic filler like 'Lorem ipsum'. Every such string is non-empty, contains real text nodes, is valid HTML, and therefore PASSES the presence rule (2779a5) and looks like a legitimate title to any structural checker. A human instantly recognizes the string as boilerplate/placeholder; judging it as a failure requires recognizing the string as a non-title AND confirming the body has substantive, identifiable content the title ignores. This is the most concrete present-but-useless category F25 explicitly enumerates, and c4a8a4 never samples it.
aspects.scLimb: Limb 2 (descriptiveness): the title must identify the topic or purpose of the page. A placeholder/default/filename title is present (limb 1 passes) but identifies nothing about the actual content.
aspects.whyUncovered: c4a8a4's three failing fixtures are a sibling-topic word ('Apple' for clementines), a first-of-two wrong title, and a bare org name on a search page — none is an authoring-tool default, a filename, or filler. The presence rule 2779a5 treats any non-whitespace text as a pass, so 'Untitled Document' sails through both ACT rules. A fully-automated checker cannot reliably catch it: 'Untitled Document' is a real, valid, non-empty string; a maintainable allowlist of every IDE/CMS default and localized variant is brittle and would false-positive on legitimate pages titled e.g. 'Document Management'. Distinguishing requires understanding that the body has specific content the placeholder fails to name.

references.quote: Authoring tool default titles, such as ... "Untitled Document" ... "No Title" ... "Untitled Page" ... "New Page 1"
Filenames that are not descriptive in their own right, such as report.html or spk12.html

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build complete, content-rich, styled HTML pages whose body unambiguously identifies a specific topic, but set <title> to a placeholder/default/filename/filler string. The body must contain enough specific, real content (headings, paragraphs, product specs, form fields) that a reader can name the true topic, making the disconnect with the placeholder title obvious. Keep markup production-shaped (DOCTYPE, lang, meta charset, head with the title alongside other meta) so the gap is purely semantic, not structural. Vary the placeholder class across pages: authoring default, source filename, raw filler.
suggestedScenarios: A fully styled product-detail page for 'Acme Noise-Cancelling Headphones X9' with specs, price, and add-to-cart, whose <title> is 'Untitled Document'.
A finished blog article about composting with multiple paragraphs and an author byline, whose <title> is 'New Page 1'.
A company contact page with address, an embedded map, and a contact form, whose <title> is the literal authoring placeholder 'Enter the title of your HTML document here'.
A detailed recipe page (ingredients, numbered steps, photo) whose <title> is the source filename 'recipe-final-v2.html'.
A government tax-form instructions page with substantive content whose <title> is the non-descriptive filename 'spk12.html'.
A support knowledge-base article on resetting a password whose <title> is 'No Title'.
A fully populated news story whose <title> is the filler 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet'.

aspects.title: Topically relevant but non-distinguishing title — bare brand/section name on one item of an obvious collection
aspects.description: Beyond mere relevance, SC 2.4.2 requires that a page belonging to a set be DISTINGUISHABLE from siblings by its title. A single page can fail this on its own evidence: its title is a bare brand or section name ('Engineering Blog', 'NorthWind Outfitters', 'Help Center') while its body is clearly ONE specific item within an obvious collection (one dated blog post, one specific SKU, one chapter, one issue, one FAQ answer). The title is topically RELEVANT (it names the site/section) yet would be byte-identical on every sibling page, so it cannot distinguish this page from the others. A human reading the body sees 'Chapter 3: Cellular Respiration' but a title of just 'Intro to Biology', and infers every chapter shares that title, failing distinguishability.
aspects.scLimb: Limb 2 (descriptiveness/distinguishability): Trusted Tester Evaluate-2 and F25's templated-site example require the title to distinguish the page from other pages in the set, a sub-limb beyond bare topic relevance.
aspects.whyUncovered: The entire ACT corpus for 2.4.2 is single isolated-page fixtures; the 'set of web pages' / distinguishability dimension is, by the corpus author's own narrowness admission, 'duplicate titles across a site ... unsampled'. c4a8a4's generic-title fail ('University of Arkham') is framed as topic-irrelevance on a search page, not as a templated-duplicate distinguishability failure where the title IS site-relevant but non-unique. An automated single-page tool cannot detect duplication without crawling, and even with a crawl, deciding whether two pages SHOULD have distinct titles (vs legitimately sharing one, like paginated views) is a semantic judgment about whether the pages have distinct topics — which the single rendered page reveals only through human inference about the collection.

references.quote: A site generated using templates includes the same title for each page on the site. So the title cannot be used to distinguish among the pages.
If the web page is part of a set of web pages, the Page Title accurately distinguishes the web page from other pages in the web site.
Be unique within the site or other resource to which the web page belongs

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build single pages whose body makes the collection membership and the specific item unmistakable (a dated post, a numbered chapter, a named SKU, an issue ID, a person's name), but set <title> to only the shared site/section/brand label that would repeat verbatim on every sibling. The judgment hinges on the reader inferring 'this title is the template constant, not the per-page variable.' Make the body's specific identifier prominent (h1, breadcrumb, metadata) so the contrast with the generic title is clear from one page.
suggestedScenarios: A single blog-post page whose body is one specific dated article ('Posted March 2, 2024: Why we migrated to Rust') but whose <title> is just 'Engineering Blog'.
A product page for one specific SKU with full specs whose <title> is only the store name 'NorthWind Outfitters'.
Chapter 3 of an online textbook, body headed 'Chapter 3: Cellular Respiration', whose <title> is just 'Intro to Biology'.
One ticket/issue detail view (issue #4821 with description and comments) whose <title> is the generic app name 'IssueTracker' with no issue identifier.
A single FAQ-answer page answering one specific question whose <title> is 'Help Center'.
A staff bio page for one named person (photo, role, bio) whose <title> is the department name 'About Our Team'.
A paginated news-listing page reading 'Page 4 of 12' in the body whose <title> is 'Latest News' with no page indicator.

aspects.title: Title makes no sense out of context — deictic/relative phrasing useless in a tab, history, site map, or search result
aspects.description: G88 and the Understanding intent center on titles consumed STRIPPED of the page body: in a tab bar, a list of open windows, browser history, a site map, or search results. A title can be accurate when you can see the page yet useless once detached: deictic/relative phrasing ('More results', 'Step 2 of 4', 'Continue', 'Details', 'Read more', 'Confirmation', 'Thank you!'), pronoun-only fragments ('About this'), or titles that only make sense relative to the previous page in a flow. On the page a sighted user has full context; the failure manifests only when the title is consumed out of context — exactly the scenario the SC is designed for. Evaluating it requires imagining the title alone in a tab/history list and asking 'would a returning user know what this page is?' — a contextual human judgment, not a string property.
aspects.scLimb: Limb 2 (descriptiveness): G88 requires the title to 'make sense when read out of context'; a deictic/relative title identifies the page only while the body is visible, defeating the out-of-context identification the SC exists for.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT fixtures only ever judge the title against the visible body on the same page, where any plausible word matches. They never simulate out-of-context consumption (tab list / search results / browser history). A title like 'Step 2' or 'Thank you' would pass c4a8a4 if the body literally is a step-2 form or a confirmation, because the words overlap — yet it fails G88's out-of-context test. Automated tools have no notion of 'out of context': they see a non-empty, even content-relevant string, so nothing fires. Recognizing that the title relies on co-present body context requires human reasoning about how the title functions when detached.

references.quote: Make sense when read out of context, for example by a screen reader or in a site map or list of search results

User agents make the title of the page easily available to the user for identifying the page. For instance, a user agent may display the page title in the window title bar or as the name of the tab containing the page.
When titles appear in site maps or lists of search results, users can more quickly identify the content they need.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages whose body is a specific, identifiable step or result in a flow, then title them with a deictic/relative fragment that is sensible mid-flow but uninterpretable alone. The body should make the on-page context rich (so c4a8a4-style lexical overlap is satisfied) while the title carries no standalone identifier (no site name, no topic, no step subject). The judgment is whether the title alone, in a tab or history list, would let a returning user identify the page.
suggestedScenarios: A multi-step checkout shipping-address form whose <title> is just 'Step 2 of 4'.
An order-confirmation page whose <title> is 'Thank you!' with no order or site identifier.
A search-results page showing more entries, titled 'More results'.
An obituary notice in a print-friendly view titled only 'Details'.
A wizard page whose body is a password-creation form, titled 'Continue'.
A software-license description page titled with the bare fragment 'About this'.
A flight-booking seat-selection page titled 'Select'.

aspects.title: Title is descriptive-shaped and topically near but states a wrong specific (stale/swapped number, date, name, or adjacent entity)
aspects.description: A subtle descriptiveness failure: the title is descriptive-SHAPED and in the right topical neighborhood, but it misrepresents the SPECIFIC content — a stale copy/paste from a sibling page, a wrong number/date/name, or a title naming a different-but-related entity. Unlike c4a8a4's 'Apple' vs 'Clementine' (an obviously different fruit named in one short sentence), real mismatches share vocabulary with the body yet state a wrong specific: an invoice page titled 'Invoice #1043' while the body shows #1044; a 2023 annual report titled 'Annual Report 2022'; a profile for 'Jordan Lee' titled 'Maria Gomez — Profile'; a 'Returns Policy' page whose body is actually the Shipping Policy. The title passes presence and looks descriptive; catching the lie requires reading the body, extracting the salient identifiers, and noticing the title contradicts them — pure human cross-checking of meaning.
aspects.scLimb: Limb 2 (descriptiveness): F25 requires the title to identify the contents of THIS page; a title that names a wrong specific (or an adjacent entity) does not identify the actual content even though it is descriptive-shaped.
aspects.whyUncovered: c4a8a4's only mismatch fixture states the topic in one plain sentence and uses a clearly different fruit — a lexical-overlap toy. It never tests a title that shares vocabulary with the body yet states a wrong specific (wrong number, date, name, or a swapped-but-adjacent topic). Automated tools cannot verify factual correspondence: 'Invoice #1043' is a valid, descriptive-looking title; confirming it should read #1044 requires parsing the body's true identifier and comparing meanings — there is no rule a checker can apply. The detection demands extracting the page's salient identifying facts and checking the title against them.

references.quote: This describes a failure condition when the web page has a title, but the title does not identify the contents or purpose of the web page.
The Page Title accurately identifies the contents or purpose of the web page
Check that the title is relevant to the content of the web page.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages where the body prominently states a specific identifier (an invoice number, a year, a person's name, a policy type, a city) and set <title> to a descriptive-shaped string that shares the surrounding vocabulary but states a contradicting specific. The mismatch must be subtle (off-by-one number, adjacent year, swapped-but-related entity), not a blatantly different topic, so that lexical-overlap heuristics pass and only a fact-level cross-check catches it.
suggestedScenarios: An invoice detail page whose body header reads 'Invoice #1044' but whose <title> is 'Invoice #1043'.
A company annual-report landing page whose body is the 2023 report but whose <title> reads 'Annual Report 2022'.
A staff profile page for 'Jordan Lee' (name, photo, role in body) whose <title> says 'Maria Gomez — Profile'.
A page whose <title> is 'Returns & Refunds Policy' but whose body is entirely the Shipping & Delivery policy.
A weather page titled 'Weather for Portland, Maine' whose body shows the forecast for Portland, Oregon.
A movie detail page titled 'The Matrix (1999)' whose body content is about 'The Matrix Reloaded (2003)'.
An event page titled 'Spring Sale — March 15' whose body announces the Summer Sale on June 20.

aspects.title: Dynamic / SPA view where the title stays frozen on a generic shell value instead of the current view's topic
aspects.description: The Understanding doc adds an explicit obligation for dynamic apps: in SPAs where distinct views are served from one URI and content changes dynamically, the title must also change to reflect the current view's topic. The failure: the app loads with a generic shell title ('My App', 'Dashboard') and, after the user navigates to a clearly distinct view (Settings, a specific record, Inbox), the rendered <title> stays frozen on the shell value. At the moment of evaluation the rendered DOM body unambiguously shows one specific view, but the title still names only the app, not the current topic — and would be identical across every view. Catching this requires understanding that the visible view has a specific topic the static title fails to reflect, and that the title did not update for this navigation.

aspects.title: Title is descriptive of the topic but in the wrong natural language for the page audience, or machine-garbled/mojibake
aspects.description: G88 requires the title to identify the subject and be usable for out-of-context identification; c4a8a4 itself lists 'Language' as a required Input Aspect, signaling descriptiveness is language-dependent. A failure mode invisible to structural tools: a page whose body is entirely in one human language while the <title> is in a different language (a localization bug where the head was not translated), a title left as an un-rendered template token, or a title that is machine-garbled/mojibake. The title may describe the topic perfectly — just not in a language the page's intended audience reading that body can use, defeating the out-of-context identification G88 is about. A human notices instantly that a German article carries an English boilerplate title, or that the title is encoding garbage; deciding whether this defeats identification for the page's audience is a semantic/linguistic judgment.
aspects.scLimb: Limb 2 (descriptiveness): G88 ties descriptiveness to out-of-context identification for the page's audience; a title in the wrong language or rendered as garbage cannot be used by that audience to identify the page, even if it nominally names the topic.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT fixture is English title + English body with overlapping words; the language-mismatch and garbled-title dimensions are never exercised, and the corpus narrowness list flags 'titles localized per lang' and 'titles containing only entities or emoji' as unsampled. Automated tools either ignore language or, at best, run language detection — but a non-English title is not per se a failure (many valid pages have foreign-language titles), so a tool cannot decide whether the title's language actually mismatches the body's audience and thereby defeats identification; that needs reading both the title and the body and reasoning about the intended audience.
